reference.source: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID) / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) recycling caused by QDPR mutations, in which dihydropteridine reductase cannot regenerate BH4 from its oxidised form

Like other BH4 disorders it presents as hyperphenylalaninaemia on newborn screening but is not corrected by dietary phenylalanine restriction alone, because dopamine and serotonin synthesis is also impaired

A distinguishing feature is secondary cerebral folate deficiency, so treatment includes folinic acid alongside neurotransmitter precursors, and untreated disease can cause intracranial calcification and a demyelinating course
Untreated children develop a progressive encephalopathy with dystonia, hypotonia, seizures, oculogyric crises, and developmental regression
Because BH4 recycling rather than synthesis is impaired, giving BH4 alone is often insufficient; management centres on controlling phenylalanine plus levodopa, a serotonin precursor, and folinic acid
The biochemical clue is normal or raised biopterin with markedly deficient dihydropteridine reductase enzyme activity, differentiating it from PTPS and GTPCH defects
reference.pathophysiology: Dihydropteridine reductase regenerates tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) from quinonoid dihydrobiopterin, sustaining the active cofactor pool. Biallelic QDPR mutations impair this recycling, so BH4 becomes functionally deficient despite adequate synthesis, disabling phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan hydroxylases. This produces hyperphenylalaninaemia together with central dopamine and serotonin deficiency. The defect additionally reduces regeneration of folate cofactors, causing cerebral folate deficiency that contributes to demyelination and basal ganglia calcification. The combined amino-acid, neurotransmitter, and folate disturbances underlie the progressive neurological deterioration seen when treatment is inadequate.
additionalDifferentials: Cerebral folate deficiency from other causes
Other neurotransmitter disorders causing infantile dystonia and encephalopathy
additionalInvestigations: Dihydropteridine reductase enzyme activity assay (deficient) in blood spots
Blood and urine pterin profile (biopterin normal or elevated) with blood phenylalanine
QDPR gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites and 5-methyltetrahydrofolate to detect cerebral folate deficiency
Brain MRI/CT for demyelination and basal ganglia calcification
BH4 loading test to characterise phenylalanine responsiveness
redFlags: Neurological regression despite good phenylalanine control, indicating untreated cofactor and folate deficiency
Seizures, dystonia, or oculogyric crises evolving in an infant with hyperphenylalaninaemia
Intracranial calcification or demyelination on neuroimaging
Failure to add folinic acid, allowing progressive cerebral folate deficiency
reference.prognosis: Early combined treatment with phenylalanine control, neurotransmitter precursors, and folinic acid can substantially improve outcome, but delayed or incomplete therapy, especially neglect of cerebral folate deficiency, leads to progressive neurological damage and disability. Lifelong metabolic follow-up is essential.
pitfalls: Managing as classic phenylketonuria and omitting the essential folinic acid and neurotransmitter therapy
Assuming BH4 supplementation alone suffices when the problem is cofactor recycling
Not measuring dihydropteridine reductase activity, so the specific recycling defect is missed
Overlooking cerebral folate deficiency and associated calcification/demyelination
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
management: Control blood phenylalanine through dietary phenylalanine restriction, recognising that diet alone is insufficient because neurotransmitter synthesis is also impaired
Replace neurotransmitter precursors with levodopa combined with a decarboxylase inhibitor and a serotonin precursor such as 5-hydroxytryptophan
Add folinic acid to treat the secondary cerebral folate deficiency and prevent demyelination and intracranial calcification
Note that tetrahydrobiopterin supplementation alone is often inadequate because the defect lies in recycling rather than synthesis
Manage seizures and dystonia symptomatically with physiotherapy and developmental support
Monitor cerebrospinal fluid neurotransmitter metabolites and blood phenylalanine with regular developmental assessment
Genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive inheritance, with lifelong metabolic follow-up
